surface_summary: A man is found murdered, staked down near an Indian reservation, with suspicion falling on local Indians and a half-breed bootlegger. The Indian agent Walter Lowell investigates amid local prejudice and intrigue involving a mysterious ranch, a threatening trader, and a young woman connected to the victim.
accepted_facts: Edward B. Sargent was found murdered and staked down on the prairie.
Jim McFann and Fire Bear were arrested as suspects.
Bill Talpers was a trader and bootlegger involved with McFann.
The murdered man was robbed of money and valuables.
inferred_conclusions: The Indians and Jim McFann committed the murder.
Bill Talpers was innocent and only a victim of circumstance.
The murder was a random act of violence by bootleggers.
mechanism_description: Edward B. Sargent killed his twin brother Willis Morgan in self-defense during a confrontation on the Dollar Sign road. To cover up the crime, Sargent staged the body of Morgan, tying it with the victim's own tent stakes and rope to suggest an Indian attack. He impersonated Morgan to maintain the deception. Bill Talpers, involved in bootlegging and theft, robbed the body and was later killed by Jim McFann after being double-crossed.
delivery_path: Sargent encounters Morgan on the road and kills him with a sawed-off shotgun.
Sargent uses Morgan's tent stakes and rope to stake down Morgan's body on the prairie.
Sargent impersonates Morgan to mislead others and maintain control of the ranch.
Talpers arrives at the murder scene, robs the body, and hides stolen money and a watch.
Talpers deceives McFann about the loot, leading to a falling out.
McFann kills Talpers after discovering the betrayal.
Sargent's horse rolls in mud near the murder scene, leaving a branded impression that reveals the truth.
outcome_result: Edward B. Sargent confesses to the murder and impersonation, clearing the innocent accused and resolving the mystery.

false_assumption.statement: The Indians and Jim McFann were guilty of the murder on the Dollar Sign road.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The presence of Indian pony tracks and moccasin prints around the body, combined with local prejudice and circumstantial evidence, made the Indians and McFann prime suspects. The staking down of the body suggested an Indian ritual, reinforcing this belief.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It conceals the fact that the real murderer was Edward B. Sargent, who staged the scene to frame the Indians and impersonated his twin brother to evade suspicion.

supporting_points: McFann was found near the murder scene.
Rope used to tie the victim was cut from McFann's lariat.
McFann had a motive related to bootlegging and was hostile.
Public opinion and local authorities strongly suspected him.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: McFann's testimony and alibi, supported by Fire Bear and other evidence, proved he was not the murderer and was manipulated by Talpers.

red_herrings.description: Indian pony tracks and Fire Bear's group were found near the murder scene, suggesting their involvement.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: They came upon the body after the murder and left tracks while investigating, but were not involved in the crime.

red_herrings.description: Bill Talpers held up a letter from Helen Ervin, using it to threaten and control her.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: While Talpers was a villain in other respects, the letter hold-up was a separate act of intimidation and not directly related to the murder mechanism.

closed_circle.rationale: The suspects were limited to those with access to the reservation and the murder scene, and who had motives or suspicious behavior connected to the crime.

discriminating_test.design: Examine the mud imprint near the murder scene for the Greek letter brand matching the old white horse at the ranch. Confirm the presence of the branded horse at the time of murder to link the rider to the crime. Cross-reference witness statements about the horse and rider's presence.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The branded horse's imprint proves that the murderer was the rider of the horse, who was impersonating Willis Morgan.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: Presence of the Greek letter brand imprint in mud at the murder scene matching the old white horse proves the rider's identity and implicates Edward B. Sargent.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed descriptions of the murder scene, including the staking down of the body and the presence of the branded horse's tracks. Testimonies from multiple witnesses, including McFann and Fire Bear, provide alibis and conflicting accounts. The letter from Helen and Talpers's suspicious behavior are presented openly. The key clue—the branded horse's imprint in the mud—is described and accessible to the reader, allowing deduction of the true murderer. The final confession confirms the solution without introducing new facts.
